posts.title: Nscale and Anthropic are reportedly in talks for yet another $45B compute deal | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lucas Ropek
posts.summary: Anthropic and AI infrastructure firm Nscale are reportedly close to finalizing a second $45 billion compute deal, following a similar agreement a little over a month ago. The new partnership would further cement Anthropic’s strategy of securing massive compute resources to fuel its generative‑AI models. Both companies are also preparing for public listings, with Anthropic expected to go public this year and Nscale facing investor pushback over a $30 billion valuation. The escalating spend on compute has drawn criticism from some investors who worry that the costs outweigh the returns, but Anthropic remains confident the investment will pay off.
key_points: Anthropic and Nscale may sign a second $45 billion compute deal
The deal follows a prior $45 billion agreement, part of Anthropic’s series of large compute partnerships
Both firms are pursuing IPOs, with Nscale encountering valuation pushback
Investor concerns about high compute spending persist despite Anthropic’s confidence

posts.title: AI assistant startup Town nabs unicorn valuation 4 months after launch | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Town, a San Francisco‑based AI assistant startup, secured a $108 million Series B round that pushed its valuation past the $1 billion unicorn threshold, just four months after its public launch. The funding, co‑led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures and joined by Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures and First Round Capital, brings the company’s total capital raised to at least $160 million. Town’s product, called a Townie, gives each employee a personalized AI assistant that connects to emails, calendars and other core work systems, and can now collaborate with customers and share approved information across the organization. In addition to the funding, Town announced a shared workflow that automatically updates employees’ Townies with new business data, eliminating the need for manual updates by each worker.
key_points: Town raised $108 million in Series B, achieving a unicorn valuation within four months of launch
The company reached millions of annual recurring revenue in weeks after its public debut
Townies are AI assistants that integrate with business tools and can collaborate with customers and each other
A new shared workflow feature automates updates to Townies, streamlining information flow

posts.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world | TechCrunch
posts.author: Rebecca Bellan
posts.summary: Laplace Intelligence is developing automated red‑teaming tools that use high‑fidelity simulations and AI agents to stress‑test robotics and autonomous systems before they are deployed in the real world. The company, founded by former University of Michigan researchers, leverages a post‑trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos platform to recreate realistic environments and generate interactive corner cases from real‑world data. Laplace is already generating revenue from autonomous trucking clients such as Bot Auto and a major Japanese automaker, and is partnering with Nvidia and T‑Mobile on a smart‑city pilot in San Jose. The startup will compete in Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, hoping to raise funds and scale its technology to compete with larger players like Applied Intuition.
key_points: Laplace uses AI agents to automatically design corner cases in realistic simulations, moving human testers out of the loop.
The startup’s high‑fidelity simulation is built on Nvidia’s Cosmos platform and incorporates real‑world map and traffic data.
Laplace already has paying customers in autonomous trucking and is partnering on a smart‑city pilot with Nvidia and T‑Mobile.
The company aims to raise capital at TechCrunch Disrupt to transition from project‑based contracts to recurring revenue.

posts.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Rivian's next act | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe is steering the company beyond just electric trucks toward a tech‑supplier model that includes AI, autonomy, and silicon. The automaker has built its own AI assistant, a 5‑nm processor with Arm and TSMC, and a full autonomous stack in partnership with Uber, while a $5.8 billion joint venture with VW focuses on electric architecture and software. Scaringe also spun out a micromobility startup called Also and owns 31 % of Mind Robotics, a robotics firm that will supply robots to Rivian factories and other customers. By licensing its technology to other brands and pursuing robotaxi deployments, Rivian aims to become a major tech supplier in the decade ahead.
key_points: Rivian is expanding from EV maker to tech supplier with AI, autonomy, and custom silicon
The company partners with Uber for autonomous driving and has a $5.8 billion joint venture with VW on electric architecture
Scaringe owns 31 % of Mind Robotics and spun out Also, broadening the company’s reach into robotics and micromobility
Rivian plans to license its tech to other brands and launch robotaxi services to grow its influence

posts.title: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Tolan, an AI companion that helps users manage daily tasks and emotions, has secured an additional $30 million in funding, bringing its total capital raised to $120 million and pushing its valuation past $268 million according to PitchBook. The company now reports double‑digit million annual recurring revenue and boasts more than 250,000 active users who have engaged in over 70 million conversations in the past year, with a user base that is 70 % women and 40 % parents. Tolan’s cartoonish avatar offers tiered memberships for full feature access, positioning it as a more approachable alternative to other AI companions that have faced criticism or bankruptcy. The startup now faces growing competition from newer AI agents like Meta’s Muse and must navigate legal risks associated with providing emotional support through AI.
key_points: Tolan raised $30 million, raising total capital to $120 million and valuation above $268 million
The app has 250,000+ active users, 70 million conversations, and double‑digit million ARR
It competes with newer AI agents such as Meta’s Muse and follows the bankruptcy of Character.AI
Legal concerns arise from lawsuits over AI‑provided emotional support

posts.title: Tenstorrent hits $6.2B valuation to scale open-weight AI chips | TechCrunch
posts.author: Marina Temkin
posts.summary: Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on inference, raised $1.5 billion in a round that lifted its valuation to $6.2 billion, more than doubling the $2.6 billion it fetched in late 2024. The funding was led by Trace Capital and Innovation X, with participation from Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price. CEO Jim Keller said the company chose to stay independent after its Galaxy servers demonstrated the ability to run DeepSeek models, and the new capital will be used to scale chips designed for open‑weight AI models and video generation. The move places Tenstorrent among a growing cohort of AI hardware startups challenging Nvidia’s dominance in the market.
key_points: $1.5B round lifts Tenstorrent’s valuation to $6.2B, doubling its previous $2.6B valuation
The round was led by Trace Capital and Innovation X, with Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price as backers
CEO Jim Keller cited Galaxy servers running DeepSeek models as a reason to remain independent
Funds will be used to scale chips for open‑weight AI models and video generation, positioning Tenstorrent against Nvidia

posts.title: Musk pledges to give 'every kid in America' one of his SpaceX shares | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Elon Musk announced that he will give one share of SpaceX to every child in the United States in 2027, a move that would be worth more than $10 billion based on the current $146 share price and represent roughly 1% of his $1 trillion net worth. He said the shares would be distributed directly to the public, possibly using Trump Accounts that accept stock donations, though the exact mechanism remains unclear. The pledge came hours after Anthropic announced a public‑benefit fund that will donate 5% of its shares to nonprofits or direct distributions, prompting Musk to suggest a similar direct‑to‑public approach. Musk’s philanthropic history has largely been channeled through the Musk Foundation, which has been criticized for funneling a large portion of its funds to entities tied to him.
key_points: Musk pledges to donate one SpaceX share to each U.S. child in 2027, valued over $10 billion
The distribution would be direct to the public, possibly via Trump Accounts
The announcement followed Anthropic’s public‑benefit fund plan, sparking a call for direct public donations
Musk’s past giving has largely flowed through the Musk Foundation, with significant internal transfers

posts.title: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Apple has tightened its developer guidelines to ban apps that use AI to generate offensive content and to prevent apps that masquerade as normal during review but later reveal nudification features. The new rules require apps that host user‑generated content to filter objectionable material, provide reporting tools, and allow users to block abusive accounts. Apple will remove any app that adds hidden or undocumented features after approval, and it has reinforced bans on apps that promote human trafficking or child exploitation. The update follows a July San Francisco court order and earlier reports that nudify apps were still available in the App Store.
key_points: Apple bans AI‑generated offensive content and apps that hide nudification features after review
New guidelines require filtering, reporting, and blocking for user‑generated content
Apple will remove apps that add hidden features post‑approval
The move follows a San Francisco court order and prior nudify app reports

posts.title: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: Benchmark announced a $2 billion raise across two funds this summer, marking only the second time in its 31‑year history that the firm has moved away from smaller vehicles. At TechCrunch Disrupt, the firm’s five partners highlighted a deliberate, low‑volume investment approach, making only two or three new bets per partner each year while maintaining a close‑knit, founder‑centric culture. Their Monday meetings run without a formal agenda, allowing the partners to stay reactive and collaborative in a rapidly changing market. The new growth fund expands Benchmark’s mandate beyond early‑stage deals, but the firm remains focused on concentrated, high‑impact investments.
key_points: Benchmark raised $2 billion across two funds, the second time in 31 years it has deviated from smaller vehicles
Partners invest only 2–3 new bets per partner per year, emphasizing a low‑volume, founder‑first strategy
Meetings are agenda‑free, fostering a collaborative and reactive decision‑making process
The new growth fund broadens opportunities but still aims for concentrated, high‑impact deals

posts.title: Everyone’s watching the Elizabeth Holmes documentary ‘You Can See Everything’ | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: The documentary "You Can See Everything" about Elizabeth Holmes has become a box‑office sensation, pulling in a $15 million opening weekend and ranking as the second‑largest opening for a documentary. The nearly three‑hour film, released after a secret screening at Telluride, is playing in only 855 theaters but has already sold out 2,000 showings and holds a 99 % rating on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic. Filmmakers were granted unprecedented access to Holmes and her family in the month before her 11‑year prison sentence, and the project was co‑directed by comedian Nathan Fielder, adding a surreal, meta‑textual layer. The film’s success has eclipsed other tech‑centric releases such as "The Social Reckoning" and Alex Gibney’s "Musk," underscoring Holmes’s enduring public fascination.
key_points: $15 million opening weekend, the second‑largest for a documentary
99 % rating on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic
Unprecedented access to Holmes and her family, co‑directed by Nathan Fielder

posts.title: TikTok says it's restored ‘Musk’ documentary advertising account | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: TikTok has restored the advertising account for the four‑hour documentary "Musk" after an error, following a temporary suspension for political content. Meta and YouTube also initially rejected ads for the film but later lifted the bans, citing technical mistakes. Elon Musk’s own platform X has declined to run any ads for the documentary. The film, directed by Alex Gibney, is expanding its theatrical run and is slated to stream on HBO next year.
key_points: TikTok restored the "Musk" ad account after an error
Meta and YouTube initially rejected ads but later allowed them
X refuses to carry ads for the documentary
The film is moving forward with broader release and HBO streaming

posts.title: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India's hospital economics | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a Series B round led by Khosla Ventures, valuing the Indian health‑tech startup at $300 million and tripling its valuation in 18 months. The company is building its own hospitals in Bengaluru, paying doctors fixed salaries and focusing on patient outcomes, which has led to less than 1% readmission rates, 40% shorter stays, and savings of over ₹500 million for insurers. Despite individual hospitals turning profitable, Even remains loss‑making with a net loss of ₹902 million in fiscal 2025, but it plans to open five more hospitals in the next six months. Khosla Ventures sees Even’s model as a scalable, outcome‑based alternative to India’s current fee‑for‑service hospital economics.
key_points: Even Healthcare secured a $50M Series B led by Khosla Ventures, valuing the firm at $300M.
The startup builds its own hospitals, pays doctors fixed salaries, and has achieved <1% readmission and 40% shorter stays.
Even’s hospitals are profitable, yet the company posted a ₹902M net loss in fiscal 2025 and is expanding rapidly.
Khosla Ventures views Even’s outcome‑driven model as a scalable alternative to India’s fee‑for‑service hospital system.

posts.title: Disney agrees to hire the majority of Character AI’s workforce | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Disney has agreed to hire the majority of Character.AI's workforce after the chatbot startup filed for bankruptcy. The deal, revealed in a legal filing, will see Disney make employment offers to at least 60 former Character.AI employees with an estimated $60 million in annual compensation, while the company had previously announced a $20 million asset acquisition. Character.AI's CEO Karandeep Anand has joined Disney as its first CTO, and most of the offered positions were accepted, though the arrangement remains a stalking‑horse bid that could be outbid. The move comes amid Character.AI's financial struggles and regulatory scrutiny over child safety concerns.
key_points: Disney will hire at least 60 former Character.AI employees, representing the majority of the startup’s workforce.
The agreement includes an estimated $60 million in annual compensation for those hires.
Character.AI’s CEO Karandeep Anand has joined Disney as its first CTO.
The deal is a stalking‑horse bid, meaning another company could potentially make a higher offer.

posts.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Replit has announced that OpenAI’s ChatGPT will become the default AI model on its cloud‑based coding platform, citing lower cost and better performance compared to Anthropic’s Claude models. The company clarified that Anthropic models will still be available, and the partnership is not fully terminated, but OpenAI is now the preferred partner for powering Replit Agent. CEO Amjad Masad highlighted a shift in Replit’s revenue mix, with enterprise contracts rising from 2% to 15% this year and an expectation that over half of revenue will come from enterprise and government customers by 2027. He also stressed the need for robust AI safety measures and infrastructure to support safe deployment of AI agents.
key_points: Replit is defaulting to OpenAI’s ChatGPT over Anthropic, driven by cost and performance advantages
Anthropic models remain available and the partnership is not fully ended
Replit’s revenue is increasingly driven by enterprise and B2B contracts, projected to exceed 50% by 2027
The CEO emphasized the importance of AI safety, orchestration, and sandboxing for secure agent deployment

posts.title: Amazon to fund 12 small nuclear reactors at former Indiana coal plant | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Amazon has announced it will fund a 960‑megawatt nuclear plant in Indiana, consisting of 12 Xe‑100 small modular reactors supplied by X‑energy and operated by American Electric Power. The company led a $700 million Series C‑1 round in X‑energy in October 2024 and plans to build 5 GW of new nuclear capacity in the U.S. by 2039. The Indiana plant will sit on the site of a demolished coal plant south of Terre Haute, connect to the public grid, and also supply power to Amazon’s data centers. The project’s timeline hinges on X‑energy’s first plant at Seadrift, Texas, which is still awaiting final NRC approval amid a lawsuit over regulatory compliance.
key_points: Amazon will fund 12 Xe‑100 SMRs at a former Indiana coal plant, creating a 960‑MW nuclear facility.
Amazon led a $700 million Series C‑1 investment in X‑energy and aims for 5 GW of nuclear capacity by 2039.
The Indiana plant will connect to the grid and power Amazon data centers, but its progress depends on X‑energy’s Seadrift project facing legal challenges.
This deal is three times larger than Amazon’s previous agreement with X‑energy.

posts.title: Tressfecta wants to make hair braiding a less arduous task for hairstylists | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Tressfecta, founded by Aisata Diallo, is developing a device called Plait Pilot that automates the hair‑separation step before braiding, a process that can take hours and cause physical strain for stylists. Diallo, a lifelong braider who stopped due to the toll on her body, built the prototype after noticing a lack of tools for textured hair. The company is still pre‑launch, bootstrapped and seeking fundraising, and it showcased the prototype at TechCrunch Disrupt to gather feedback from professional braiders.
key_points: Tressfecta’s Plait Pilot automates hair separation to speed up braiding and reduce physical strain on stylists
Founder Aisata Diallo created the device after experiencing pain from manual braiding
The product is still in prototype, pre‑launch, and the company is preparing to raise funds
Tressfecta presented its prototype at TechCrunch Disrupt and is engaging stylists for testing

posts.title: Scimplify raises $25M to challenge China's grip on critical materials with AI | TechCrunch
posts.author: Jagmeet Singh
posts.summary: Scimplify, an Indian AI‑driven specialty‑chemicals startup, closed a $25 million all‑equity round led by Hitachi Ventures with new investors Henkel and Teknor Apex, valuing the company at $250 million. The funding will accelerate its Scinode platform, which can deliver custom materials in about two months—far faster than the typical 12‑18‑month timeline—by mapping production routes and quality requirements across a network of 500+ facilities. Scimplify is targeting $400 million in annualized revenue, expanding its manufacturing footprint to the U.S. and Japan, and focusing on critical materials such as tungsten derivatives and rare‑earths to reduce dependence on China. The company’s current run rate is $200 million, already EBITDA‑positive, and it serves over 1,000 customers in more than 40 countries.
key_points: $25 million all‑equity round led by Hitachi Ventures values Scimplify at $250 million
Scinode AI platform cuts material development time from 12‑18 months to about two months
Company focuses on critical materials like tungsten derivatives and rare‑earths to diversify supply chains away from China
Scimplify’s annualized revenue run rate is $200 million, targeting $400 million and is EBITDA‑positive

posts.title: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Meta updated its commercial terms of use to allow the company to use content from business account domains, web pages, or URLs for product development, research, training, and maintenance of its services. Legal experts interpreted this clause as a potential permission for Meta to scrape publisher websites and use the material to train its AI models, raising concerns about copyright and data usage. Meta stated that the update did not alter its web‑crawling practices, but The Verge later reported that the clause has been removed from the terms. The episode underscores the ongoing debate over AI training data and the legal boundaries of web scraping.
key_points: Meta added a clause permitting use of business account domain content for AI training and product development.
Legal experts warned the clause could enable broad web scraping of publisher sites.
Meta clarified the update did not change its crawling behavior.
The clause was subsequently removed from the commercial terms of use.

posts.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings | TechCrunch
posts.author: Anthony Ha
posts.summary: Anthropic’s latest internal report shows a shift toward a more experienced workforce, with junior technical hires falling from 27% to 9% and overall junior staff dropping from 21% to 14% since early 2025. The company’s technical teams now make up only 56% of its employees, a decline attributed to business‑function expansion and coding tools that enable non‑technical staff to build software. Meeting time has risen 20% overall and 16% for technical contributors, as employees cite the need for human trust and accountability when coordinating Claude‑generated outputs. While Claude has increased productivity—more code per person, higher sales per rep, and faster contract processing—employees report a bottleneck in reviewing the large volume of text it produces, indicating that human attention remains a limiting factor.
key_points: Junior technical hires dropped from 27% to 9% and overall junior staff from 21% to 14% since early 2025
Meeting time per employee rose 20% (16% for technical staff) as coordination around Claude becomes essential
Claude boosts productivity but creates an attention bottleneck as employees must sift through its output
Technical teams now represent 56% of the workforce, reflecting a shift toward business functions and non‑technical coding tools

posts.title: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Ember has released its third‑generation temperature‑controlled mug, the Mug 3, which adds on‑mug button controls and a sliding lid, and can keep drinks hot for up to three hours on a single charge. The new mug eliminates the need to open the app to adjust temperature, letting users cycle through five preset temperatures from 125°F to 145°F with a button on the bottom. It is available in 10‑ounce ($129) and 14‑ounce ($149) sizes, comes in multiple colors, and is the first Ember mug that is top‑rack dishwasher‑safe. Alongside the mug, Ember also launched the Tumbler 2, a 16‑ounce travel mug priced at $179, expanding its lineup of smart drinkware.
key_points: Mug 3 adds a bottom‑mounted button that cycles through five preset temperatures, removing the need for app interaction.
The mug can maintain temperature for up to three hours on a single charge and is top‑rack dishwasher‑safe.
It is available in 10‑oz ($129) and 14‑oz ($149) sizes, with a range of color options.

posts.title: Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept | TechCrunch
posts.author: Connie Loizos
posts.summary: Mark Wahlberg is launching Municipal Gym, a 32,000-square-foot club in Las Vegas that opens in December and offers diagnostics, recovery gear, a café, and a community‑focused wellness experience at a lower price point than high‑end longevity clubs. The gym builds on his earlier Municipal apparel line and reflects his desire to impact health beyond apparel, providing blood work, doctor consultations, supplements, and hormone therapy for about $99 a month. Wahlberg plans aggressive expansion, citing favorable landlord terms and a vision of a wellness ecosystem that contrasts with the “join‑up but don’t show up” model of many gyms. The venture signals his shift from acting to health entrepreneurship, aiming to inspire underserved youth while keeping the brand’s public‑service ethos.
key_points: Wahlberg’s Municipal Gym will open in December in Las Vegas, offering diagnostics, recovery tools, and a café at a lower price point than luxury longevity clubs.
The gym is part of a broader Municipal ecosystem that began with a sportswear line and now includes supplements, hormone therapy, and a community‑focused wellness model.
Wahlberg plans aggressive expansion, leveraging favorable landlord terms and a vision to inspire underserved youth and create a supportive fitness community.

posts.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kirsten Korosec
posts.summary: Replit has shifted its default AI model from Anthropic to OpenAI, citing cost, performance, and partnership strength. CEO Amjad Masad announced at TechCrunch Disrupt that while Anthropic models remain available, ChatGPT will be the default for Replit Agent. The move follows an August partnership with OpenAI and reflects Replit’s broader strategy to grow enterprise revenue, which now accounts for a larger share of its business. Despite the change, Replit remains model‑agnostic and continues to support Anthropic’s Claude models for users who choose them.
key_points: Replit will use OpenAI’s ChatGPT as the default model, though Anthropic models stay available.
The switch is driven by cost savings, better performance on benchmarks, and a stronger partnership with OpenAI.
Enterprise contracts now represent a growing portion of Replit’s revenue, projected to dominate by 2027.
Replit maintains a model‑agnostic stance, allowing users to select from Claude, OpenAI, and other supported models.

posts.title: In 'You Can See Everything,' Elizabeth Holmes meets her equal in comedian Nathan Fielder | TechCrunch
posts.author: Amanda Silberling
posts.summary: Nathan Fielder and director Lance Oppenheim filmed a docu‑reality project that followed Elizabeth Holmes in the month before she began her 11‑year prison sentence, aiming to document her final days of freedom and reshape her public image. The film interweaves Holmes’ own attempts to exonerate herself—through an A24 partnership and an AI avatar of her created by her husband—with the meta‑layer of actress Amanda Seyfried, who portrays Holmes in the Hulu miniseries "The Dropout". By juxtaposing Holmes’ real‑world testimony, her staged reactions to Seyfried’s portrayal, and the legal context of her trial, the documentary exposes the blurred line between her constructed persona and the facts of her fraud. The result is a commentary on how media, performance, and legal narratives collide to shape public perception of a controversial figure.
key_points: Fielder and Oppenheim filmed Holmes in a docu‑reality project during the last month of her freedom to document her final days
Holmes and her husband used an A24 partnership and an AI avatar to shape her narrative, while actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in "The Dropout" adds a meta layer
The film highlights the blurred line between Holmes’ constructed persona and the facts of her fraud, questioning her innocence
The documentary shows how media, performance, and legal contexts collide to influence public perception

posts.title: Porsche’s electric Macan Turbo is an automotive existential crisis | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV is a high‑performance two‑row crossover that blends sports‑car acceleration with SUV practicality, yet its styling and option overload raise questions about its identity. With 630 horsepower, a 100‑kWh battery, and a 285‑mile range, the car can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in under four seconds while still offering a comfortable, family‑friendly interior. The price starts at $112,700 but can climb to $149,610 with options, making it one of the most expensive EVs on the market. Despite its impressive specs, the Macan’s navigation and charging guidance can be confusing, and many optional features add little value for most buyers.
key_points: The Macan Turbo EV delivers sports‑car performance in a crossover body, with 630 hp and 285‑mile range.
Its price can exceed $150,000 when fully equipped, far above comparable EVs like the Chevy Bolt.
Charging is fast—20 minutes from 19% to 80% on a 350‑kW charger—but the navigation system can misdirect users to slower chargers.
Many optional features, such as the Turbo badge and illuminated logos, add little practical benefit and inflate cost.

posts.title: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aditya Mehta
posts.summary: Elorian, a Palo Alto AI startup, has launched its first multimodal model, Glimpse, which is designed to reason with images by repeatedly accessing the source rather than converting to text tokens. The model, trained on a few hundred GPUs, offers a visual scratch space that allows it to crop, zoom, and run code during reasoning, and it is priced at $0.60 per million input tokens and $3 per million output tokens. Benchmarks show Glimpse outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short‑form video captioning while remaining smaller and cheaper than many frontier systems. Elorian plans to target video‑heavy industries and eventually extend the model to control robots, aiming to build the world’s best visual reasoning model next year.
key_points: Glimpse uses a visual scratch space to repeatedly access and manipulate image data during reasoning
The model is smaller and cheaper than many frontier multimodal systems, costing $0.60/million input and $3/million output tokens
It outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short‑form video captioning
Elorian targets video‑heavy companies and plans to add robotic control capabilities in the future

posts.title: Replit's CEO says the future of work is the 'self-driving company' | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Replit co‑founder Amjad Masad told TechCrunch Disrupt that the rise of AI is turning companies into "self‑driving" organizations where agents handle routine tasks and humans focus on judgment and design. He explained how Replit’s own support workflow now begins with an AI agent triaging tickets, letting staff make higher‑level decisions and deploy fixes with a single click. Masad emphasized that AI will not replace people but shift their work toward architecture, strategy, and creativity, making jobs less boring and more productive. The CEO also noted that conversations with other businesses center on using AI to boost employee happiness and efficiency rather than merely cutting costs.
key_points: Replit’s support system now uses AI agents to triage tickets before human intervention
AI shifts human work toward higher‑level design and decision‑making rather than replacing it
Masad envisions a future where companies are "self‑driving" with agents handling routine tasks

posts.title: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sean O'Kane
posts.summary: Tesla unveiled its redesigned second‑generation Roadster featuring SpaceX‑powered cold‑gas thrusters that allow the car to perform aerial flips, spin, and lift itself over other Tesla models during a live demo outside Waco, Texas. The vehicle can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in one second, reach speeds over 230 mph, and offers a 300‑mile range across three trims—Performance, Thrust, and Rocket—priced at $50,000, $250,000, and invite‑only, respectively. Production is slated for 2028 after a series of delays, and Musk frames the Roadster as a halo car that prioritizes spectacle over immediate revenue. The design draws inspiration from high‑speed aircraft and James Bond cars, positioning the Roadster as a futuristic, high‑performance statement vehicle.
key_points: Tesla’s second‑generation Roadster uses SpaceX cold‑gas thrusters to achieve 0‑60 mph in one second and perform aerial maneuvers during a live demo
Three trims—Performance, Thrust, Rocket—offer 300‑mile range, 230+ mph, and prices of $50,000, $250,000, with Rocket being invite‑only
The vehicle will be produced in 2028 after repeated delays, and Musk markets it as a halo car rather than a revenue driver
The design is inspired by aircraft and James Bond cars, emphasizing futuristic aesthetics and high performance

posts.title: Intero Biosystems wants drugmakers to test on mini human intestines, not animals | TechCrunch
posts.author: Kate Park
posts.summary: Intero Biosystems, a Denver‑based startup spun out of the University of Michigan, is selling 1‑millimeter human intestinal organoids called GastroScreen to replace animal models in drug testing. The company has raised $2.3 million in pre‑seed funding, generated over $400,000 in revenue in its first year, and is in the second stage of a three‑stage validation process that has already shown expected responses to known gut‑targeted drugs. FDA guidance issued this year encourages the use of non‑animal methods, boosting interest from pharma and giving Intero a window to scale production to hundreds of thousands of organoids per batch. Competitors such as Altis Biosystems and InSphero also offer gut models, but Intero differentiates itself with iPSC‑derived, scalable, and potentially personalized organoids that can be shipped directly to customers.
key_points: Intero sells 1‑mm human intestinal organoids (GastroScreen) to replace animal testing in drug development.
FDA’s 2024 guidance on non‑animal methods has increased pharma interest in organoid technologies.
Intero is in the second validation stage, demonstrating expected drug responses and planning to scale to hundreds of thousands per batch.

The Frontier, priced at $74.99, is a wrist‑worn or clip‑on device that offers IP67 water resistance, seven days of battery life, and advanced noise‑filtered microphones, while the Eclipse is a credit‑card‑sized phone attachment costing $99.99. Both devices capture conversations in real time, generate free summaries, and, with an $11.99 monthly Bee Pro subscription, provide unlimited summaries, to‑do suggestions, and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third‑party productivity apps. posts.summary: Flock’s CEO Garrett Langley told TechCrunch Disrupt that the company’s microphones only detect gunshots, a claim that contrasts with the company’s website, which advertises detection of gunfire, car crashes, fireworks and other ambient sounds. The company’s Gunshot Detection feature, launched last year, was criticized for listening to human voices; after backlash it removed the distress‑detection capability and clarified that it does not monitor conversations. Protesters in San Francisco gathered outside the venue as privacy groups and the ACLU called for tighter oversight, and several states have already ended contracts with Flock. Despite the controversy, Langley maintains that the system’s primary purpose is public‑safety alerts and that its microphone network is comparable to ShotSpotter’s 25,000‑unit array.

posts.title: Colossal Biosciences announces new AI platform to help accelerate de-extinction efforts | TechCrunch
posts.author: Dominic-Madori Davis
posts.summary: Colossal Biosciences unveiled GenoMorph, an AI platform that uses 3D morphology, comparative genomics, and developmental biology to pinpoint gene edits for extinct species with sparse genomic data, notably the dodo. The system, built on data from over 70 bird species and developmental studies of chickens, quail, ducks, and pigeons, has identified roughly 2,300 promising DNA targets for dodo cranial morphology and will test them using a lipid‑nanoparticle delivery method. In parallel, the company expanded its Nicobar pigeon colony to 36 birds and produced essential germ cells, a key step toward creating dodo‑like birds. The launch attracted backing from XPRIZE founder Peter Diamandis, who announced a new VC firm, NeoGenesis Capital, to support Colossal’s programmable biology platform across health, agriculture, and conservation.

posts.title: Ambrosia Energy will build a 10 GWh factory in Texas to make batteries for off-grid data centers | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant

The 150,000‑square‑foot facility is expected to reach full production in two to three years, following the startup’s stealth launch in June and its sale of the Swarm satellite constellation to SpaceX. Ambrosia’s first commercial plant, slated for West Texas later this year, will combine 300 MW of solar panels with 660 MWh of batteries to deliver 30 MW of continuous power and a 99.3% uptime target. posts.author: Tim De Chant

The rebound is driven by competitive pricing, higher gasoline costs, and a surge in demand for models such as Toyota’s refreshed bZ and Lexus RZ, which doubled sales after adding Tesla‑style charging ports and larger batteries. Despite a 20% year‑over‑year decline, Tesla remains the dominant player, accounting for more than half of all EV sales in the third quarter. The U.S. recovery mirrors Germany’s post‑incentive rebound, where sales fell sharply after the 2023 incentive cut but then steadily recovered to near‑record levels.

posts.title: Deezer will soon let you filter out AI-generated music | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Deezer announced it will launch a toggle that lets users filter out AI‑generated music from search results, a feature slated for release before year‑end. The move follows a 2023 survey where 45% of users wanted to remove AI tracks, and the platform has seen AI content rise from 10% of daily uploads to over 50% in July. Deezer’s CEO Alexis Lanternier said the option will let listeners focus on human‑created music if they choose. The change comes amid a broader industry debate, with competitors like Bandcamp banning AI tracks and Spotify only tagging them.
key_points: Deezer introduces a toggle to filter AI‑generated music, expected before year‑end
45% of users surveyed want to remove AI tracks; AI uploads rose from 10% to over 50% of daily uploads
Competitors have varied policies: Bandcamp bans AI tracks, Tidal cuts monetization, Spotify tags them

posts.title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Science Corporation announced that it has implanted its vision‑restoring chip PRIMA into the first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited retinal disorder that destroys central vision. The patient, treated at Sydney Eye Hospital in May, was able to see a letter during the first rehabilitation session and read a word in the second, demonstrating the chip’s early efficacy. PRIMA, already sold in Europe for geographic atrophy, works by placing a small implant in the back of the eye and using camera‑equipped glasses to transmit visual information directly to the retina. The company, founded by former Neuralink executive Max Hodak, views this success as a step toward broader brain‑computer interface applications beyond vision restoration.
key_points: First Stargardt patient received PRIMA chip and saw letters and words during rehab
PRIMA is already commercially available in Europe for geographic atrophy
Science Corporation aims to expand BCI technology beyond vision to other neurological conditions
The implant uses a small chip and camera glasses to act as artificial photoreceptors

posts.title: Cerebras CEO says we're nearing a future where everyone has a personal AI assistant at home | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Cerebras Systems CEO Andrew Feldman announced that personal AI assistants are likely to become common home appliances in the near future. He explained that these assistants would operate both locally and in the cloud, featuring strong security perimeters and the ability to handle financial transactions. Feldman highlighted the rapid progress of consumer AI agents such as Meta’s Muse and Instinct, and noted that he personally uses a suite of agents to manage his schedule and information. He emphasized that his company’s focus is on building the hardware infrastructure that will enable other innovators to create the next generation of home AI experiences.
key_points: Cerebras CEO predicts personal AI assistants will soon be common home appliances
These assistants will run locally and in the cloud with security and credit‑card capabilities
Feldman uses agents himself and focuses on infrastructure for others
Consumer AI agents like Meta’s Muse and Instinct illustrate rapid progress

posts.title: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks | TechCrunch
posts.author: Aisha Malik
posts.summary: Industrial Next, a San Francisco startup founded by former Tesla engineers, unveiled AI‑driven robotic stations that can be reconfigured in minutes instead of weeks, enabling factories to switch tasks quickly. The company demonstrated its technology at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and announced a partnership with BMW Group Technology Office to evaluate its dexterous manipulation for manufacturing. By training robots in high‑fidelity simulated environments, Industrial Next’s stations can perform delicate tasks—such as threading flex cables and peeling protective film from camera modules—at or above human speed with 100% accuracy. The founders aim to extend this flexibility to complex, end‑to‑end production, ultimately enabling fully automated car manufacturing without human touch.
key_points: Industrial Next’s robotic stations can be reconfigured in minutes, dramatically reducing downtime for task changes.
The startup uses high‑fidelity simulation to train robots for high‑precision, dexterous tasks without needing extensive real‑world data.
A partnership with BMW Group Technology Office is underway to test the technology in automotive manufacturing.
The founders, ex‑Tesla engineers, are targeting fully automated production lines for complex products like smartphones and cars.

posts.title: Cerebras CEO pushes back on AI doomsday warnings | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Cerebras Systems CEO Andrew Feldman criticized the growing AI doomsday narrative, arguing it distracts from the technology’s potential benefits. He urged industry leaders to emphasize positive outcomes—such as eliminating diseases—while still acknowledging and regulating risks. Feldman also blamed the data‑center sector’s poor community engagement for fueling NIMBY backlash and called for more collaborative approaches to new AI‑driven infrastructure. Despite his optimism, he acknowledged that powerful AI will inevitably attract misuse and must be handled responsibly.
key_points: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman criticized AI doomsday warnings at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.
He urged the industry to highlight AI’s benefits, like disease prevention, while still regulating risks.
Feldman blamed data‑center community engagement failures for NIMBY backlash and called for better collaboration.
He acknowledged that powerful AI will attract misuse and must be responsibly managed.

posts.title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim Fernholz
posts.summary: Longshot Space Technology is developing a ground‑based multi‑injection gun that can accelerate projectiles to hypersonic speeds, with the goal of turning the gun into a reusable launch vehicle. The Alameda‑based startup has raised about $20 million, is testing a 70‑foot, 6‑inch gun that reaches Mach 4 and plans a 3,000‑foot, 30‑inch gun capable of launching 220‑lb payloads at Mach 8, while also providing hypersonic test services for the U.S. military. Longshot envisions a 10‑km gun that could loft payloads to orbital velocity, potentially cutting launch costs to roughly $50 per kilogram—well below the $300 per kilogram threshold needed for the orbital data‑center market. The company’s progress hinges on securing suitable test sites, but its reusable, low‑fuel design offers a compelling alternative to conventional rockets.
key_points: Longshot’s multi‑injection gun can reach Mach 8 and launch 220‑lb payloads, aiming to reduce launch costs to $50/kg
The startup has raised $20 million and holds U.S. military contracts for hypersonic testing
Future plans include a 3,000‑ft gun and a 10‑km gun that could place payloads into orbit
Site availability remains a major challenge for scaling the technology

posts.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ram Iyer
posts.summary: Pluto Security, a stealth‑mode startup that began selling its AI‑security platform in April, has closed a $42 million Series A led by Jump Capital, bringing its total funding to $42 million. The company argues that the rapid adoption of generative‑AI tools in enterprises creates new, hard‑to‑detect security holes, noting that about 60 % of the risks it finds come from non‑developer‑coded applications, especially in finance, marketing and legal departments. Pluto’s solution monitors AI agents in real time, intercepting risky actions and enforcing policies without stopping employees from using AI, and it already reports $2 million in annual recurring revenue from more than 30 enterprise customers such as Oscar Health and AlphaSense. The funding will be used to expand product development, security research and the company’s U.S. presence.
key_points: Pluto Security raised $42 million in a Series A, adding to an $8.5 million seed round
The firm claims 60 % of the security risks it detects stem from AI tools coded by non‑developers, especially in finance, marketing and legal teams
Pluto’s platform monitors AI agent behavior in real time, allowing interventions before dangerous actions are completed

posts.title: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: Google Play has introduced a feature that lets users build and run private, vibe‑coded apps on their Android devices through Google Play without publishing them publicly. The apps, created with Google AI Studio, stay hidden from search and listing pages and are only accessible to the creator, though they must still meet Play’s policy guidelines. Initially available to U.S. users 18 and older, the service will later allow sharing with a limited network of trusted friends and, if desired, a transition to a public Play Store listing after a safety review. The move reflects Google’s push to make app development more personal and secure, complementing other AI‑driven enhancements such as Game Finder and Ask Play.
key_points: Private vibe‑coded apps can now be launched on Android via Google Play without public listing.
Feature available to U.S. users 18+ and will later support sharing with trusted friends.
Apps must still comply with Play policies and can be moved to public listing after review.

posts.title: Licube wants to be the fuel provider to the fusion power industry — see how at TechCrunch Disrupt | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Licube, a Japanese startup, has developed an electrolyzer that can enrich natural lithium to 99.995% lithium‑6, the isotope needed for tritium breeding in fusion reactors. The company argues that the scarcity of lithium‑6—only about 7.5% of natural lithium—will become a bottleneck as fusion plants seek to produce their own tritium on site. Licube estimates a $50 billion market by 2040 if fusion power becomes commercial, while also targeting semiconductor, pharmaceutical, fission, and spacecraft industries with its purification technology. The startup showcased its pitch at TechCrunch Disrupt’s Startup Battlefield, positioning itself as a key fuel supplier for the future fusion economy.
key_points: Licube’s electrolyzer can enrich lithium to 99.995% lithium‑6, essential for tritium production in fusion reactors.
Natural lithium‑6 is only 7.5% of lithium, creating a supply gap that fusion plants will need to overcome.
Licube projects a $50 billion market by 2040 if fusion power comes online.
Until fusion is viable, the company plans to serve semiconductor, pharmaceutical, fission, and spacecraft markets with its purification tech.

posts.title: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ram Iyer
posts.summary: Flox Intelligence, a startup spun out of KTH Royal Institute of Technology, has developed edge AI devices that detect wildlife and emit species‑specific deterrent sounds to keep animals away from trains, airports, roads, and other critical infrastructure. The system uses on‑device perception models trained on wildlife behavior, learns from experience to avoid habituation, and is already deployed in about 150 units across North America, Europe, and Australia. Flox sells the hardware upfront and then charges an annual software and AI subscription, projecting $1.5 million in revenue by the end of 2026. While competitors like Robin Radar and iCHASE offer similar deterrent technologies, Flox claims its advantage lies in the breadth of its data and the adaptability of its system to various outdoor environments.
key_points: Flox’s edge AI devices detect animals and emit species‑specific sounds, learning from experience to prevent habituation
The company has 150 units live worldwide and plans to scale to several thousand with a $10 million Series A
Flox’s revenue model combines upfront hardware sales with annual software subscriptions, targeting $1.5 million in 2026
Its competitive moat is the extensive field data and adaptable perception system for diverse outdoor settings

posts.title: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: MIT startup LNK Energies has developed a system that converts existing heavy‑duty diesel trucks into hydrogen‑powered haulers, reducing total cost of ownership by about 13% and cutting emissions. The technology uses liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHCs) and a compact on‑board reactor that eliminates the need for high‑pressure compression, allowing the truck to run on a conventional internal‑combustion engine or a fuel cell. LNK plans to install a larger reactor in a commercial truck within 18 months and aims to price the fuel at $6.50 per gallon after producing 50–100 units, without relying on subsidies. The company will showcase its prototype at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco.
key_points: LNK Energies turns diesel Class 8 trucks into hydrogen haulers using LOHCs and a mini‑fridge‑sized reactor.
The system removes the expensive 11,000‑psi compression step, lowering operating costs by ~13% versus diesel.
Fuel can be dispensed from standard diesel stations, avoiding new hydrogen infrastructure.
LNK targets a $6.50 per gallon price after 50–100 trucks, aiming to be cheaper even during early adoption.

posts.title: Exclusive: Cambridge Heavy Industries has been quietly building a desktop fusion device | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Cambridge Heavy Industries, a stealth startup in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has unveiled a benchtop inertial‑confinement fusion reactor that uses only two lasers to ignite a fuel target, enabling rapid iteration and AI‑driven design optimization. The modular device can perform 50 to 80 shots per day, generating data that feeds simulations to improve performance, and the company recently closed a $6.2 million seed round led by Azolla Ventures. In the next decade the firm plans to scale the prototype to a plant the size of two basketball courts, while using its smaller units to produce tritium—an expensive isotope needed for most fusion reactors. The approach could provide a new, cost‑effective source of tritium and a pathway to commercial fusion power.
key_points: Cambridge Heavy’s tabletop fusion reactor uses only two lasers, reducing complexity and cost while allowing 50–80 daily experiments
The startup’s rapid‑iteration, AI‑optimized design has attracted a $6.2 million seed round from Azolla Ventures and other investors
Future plans include scaling the device to a plant the size of two basketball courts and using it to produce tritium, which is scarce and expensive
The technology could supply a new source of tritium and accelerate the development of commercial fusion power

posts.title: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Meta has launched a new AI‑powered tool called "Your Algorithm" on Facebook that lets users shape what appears in their Feed and Reels by describing their interests in plain language. The feature works in real time, allowing users to adjust preferences and receive more relevant content, and it can prompt follow‑up questions to refine recommendations. Meta also updated the three‑dot menu so that "Your Algorithm," "Interested," and "Not interested" options are now accessible directly from individual posts. The rollout follows similar moves on Instagram and Threads, marking a broader shift toward giving users more agency over algorithmic curation.
key_points: Meta’s "Your Algorithm" lets Facebook users influence feed and Reels content through natural‑language preferences.
The tool updates recommendations in real time and may ask follow‑up questions to refine suggestions.
Facebook’s menu changes make it easier to manage preferences directly from posts.
The launch extends Meta’s personalization strategy across Instagram and Threads.

posts.title: These execs think voice AI hasn't reached its ChatGPT moment yet | TechCrunch
posts.author: Ivan Mehta
posts.summary: Voice‑AI startups have attracted billions of dollars as investors chase the next big interface, yet industry leaders say the technology still lacks a "ChatGPT moment." PolyAI’s CTO highlighted that while full‑duplex models can speak and listen simultaneously, the real hurdle is delivering fast, natural reasoning so conversations feel seamless and customers trust AI agents. Otter’s CMO emphasized that accurate transcription and speaker identification are critical for meeting‑note tools, and that transparency—clearly indicating when an AI is present—must be built into enterprise solutions. Together, these insights suggest that voice AI’s future hinges on improving ASR accuracy, reasoning speed, and user trust through clear disclosure.
key_points: Full‑duplex models exist but fast, natural reasoning is still missing
Accurate transcription and speaker ID are essential for meeting‑note AI
Transparency about AI presence is crucial for enterprise trust

posts.title: Helix Carbon says it can make iron cheaper by recycling blast furnace pollution | TechCrunch
posts.author: Tim De Chant
posts.summary: Helix Carbon has developed an electrolyzer that can convert the carbon dioxide emitted by blast furnaces into carbon monoxide, allowing iron producers to reduce their coke consumption and lower emissions. The startup claims the technology could cut coke use by 30‑90 % and save producers about $14 per ton of iron, a meaningful margin boost in an industry with thin profits. By targeting the $2 trillion steel market, Helix plans to first serve specialty‑chemical customers before scaling to full‑scale blast furnaces. The approach offers a win‑win of lower carbon output and higher profitability for iron producers.
key_points: Helix Carbon’s electrolyzer turns blast‑furnace CO₂ into CO for reuse, cutting coke use.
Potential coke reduction ranges from 30‑90 %, saving ~$14/ton of iron.
The technology offers both emission cuts and margin gains in a thin‑margin industry.
Helix plans to start with specialty‑chemical customers before targeting full blast furnaces.

posts.title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case | TechCrunch
posts.author: Sarah Perez
posts.summary: A U.S. District Judge ordered Apple to receive expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade‑secrets lawsuit Apple filed in July. The court granted Apple the right to view documents related to interviews with former Apple employees who applied to OpenAI’s consumer hardware and robotics teams, and also allowed access to private LINE messages and depositions of those employees. OpenAI must hand over already‑collected materials within five days and any remaining documents within fourteen days. Apple’s request for broader access to OpenAI’s research and development data was denied, though the judge left room for a narrowed request.
key_points: Apple gains expedited access to OpenAI hiring documents and private messages
OpenAI must turn over materials within 5 and 14 days
Judge denied Apple access to OpenAI R&D and broader discovery requests
Depositions of former Apple employees at OpenAI are approved

posts.title: What to know about the landmark Warner Bros. Discovery sale | TechCrunch
posts.author: Lauren Forristal
posts.summary: Warner Bros. Discovery agreed to sell its entire portfolio to Paramount for $111 billion, finalizing a deal that will combine studios, HBO, streaming services, games, and TV networks such as CNN and HGTV. The transaction followed a bidding war that began in October 2025, with Netflix initially offering $82.7 billion for the film and TV assets before withdrawing after Paramount raised its bid to $111 billion. The deal was cleared by the U.S. Department of Justice in June, temporarily blocked by a lawsuit from 12 state attorneys general in July, and ultimately approved by a federal judge in September, becoming official on October 6. The acquisition will be financed with a $54 billion debt commitment from major banks and $45.7 billion in equity from Larry Ellison, while raising concerns over job cuts, political influence, and antitrust scrutiny.
key_points: Paramount wins $111B bid for WBD assets
Deal faced DOJ approval, state AG lawsuit, and federal judge clearance
Financing includes $54B debt and $45.7B equity from Larry Ellison
Concerns over job cuts, political influence, and antitrust scrutiny

posts.title: FBI arrests OpenAI employee accused of planting hidden recording device in conference room | TechCrunch
posts.author: Zack Whittaker
posts.summary: OpenAI has fired and the FBI has arrested an employee, Abdulrahman Alfozan, after discovering a hidden, encrypted recording device in an executive conference room. The device, reportedly equipped with advanced encryption and audio monitoring, was found in a USB port behind a television in the San Francisco office, and prosecutors say it was intended to covertly capture sensitive conversations about the company’s super‑intelligence technology. OpenAI confirmed that Alfozan had joined in July 2025 and that there is no evidence he accessed or exfiltrated model weights, source code, or customer data. The case underscores the growing focus on counterintelligence and the protection of AI intellectual property.
key_points: FBI arrested OpenAI employee for hidden recording device
Device had advanced encryption and was placed behind a TV in the conference room
No evidence of data theft, but intended to capture sensitive AI discussions
Alfozan joined July 2025, fired Oct 9, faces up to 5 years
